title: FRISM: Fine-Grained Reasoning Injection via Subspace-Level Model Merging for Vision-Language Models
one_liner: FRISM merges a vision-language model with a reasoning model at the level of singular-value subspaces, so reasoning-heavy directions can be injected without overwriting the visual directions that the base model already handles well.
lead: Merging a vision-language model with a large reasoning model is attractive because it can transfer stronger step-by-step problem solving without retraining everything from scratch. The problem is that most merges act at the whole-layer level: they add or scale an entire update for a layer even though different directions inside that layer do different jobs. Some directions support visual perception, while others support abstract reasoning. If the merge scales all of them together, reasoning can improve while visual grounding degrades. FRISM addresses this by decomposing the reasoning update with singular value decomposition, meaning it rewrites the update as ordered subspaces whose contributions can be scaled separately. It then learns which subspaces to inject more strongly and which to damp down, using self-distillation on vision-language data so the merged model keeps perception while gaining reasoning. The paper matters because it treats model merging as selective transfer of internal directions rather than coarse averaging of whole layers.

problem.h2: Why coarse model merging damages perception
paras: A task vector, meaning the list of weight-value differences between a base model and a task-adapted model, captures how a model changed to solve a new task. Existing merge methods often add that task vector back to the base model at the layer level. That is simple, but it assumes all directions inside the layer are equally useful for the new task and equally safe for the old one.

In a vision-language model, that assumption is weak. Some internal directions matter for reading visual evidence, aligning image regions with text, or preserving spatial detail. Other directions matter more for mathematical or symbolic reasoning. If the merge injects the full reasoning update everywhere, the reasoning directions arrive together with directions that can distort perception. FRISM tries to separate those directions before merging.

callout.b: The paper's move in one sentence.
callout.html: Decompose the reasoning update into ordered subspaces, learn separate merge scales for those subspaces, and train those scales so reasoning gains are kept while visual behavior is preserved.

panels.title: 1. Base vision-language model sees well
panels.caption: The starting model is grounded in images but may not reason deeply on hard tasks.

panels.title: 2. Reasoning model adds a large update
panels.caption: The update contains several internal directions, not all of which should be merged equally.

panels.title: 3. SVD splits the update into subspaces
panels.caption: The decomposition isolates components that can be scaled independently.

panels.title: 4. Learn subspace scales from vision-language data
panels.caption: The merge keeps the directions that help reasoning and restrains the ones that would harm perception.

panels.title: 5. Final model reasons more without losing sight
panels.caption: The merged model aims for higher reasoning quality while staying visually grounded.

steps.text: Measure how the reasoning model differs from the base vision-language model in its stored weight values.
Apply singular value decomposition so the update becomes a sum of ordered subspace components.
Give each subspace component its own coefficient instead of using one layer-wide merge weight.
Use unlabeled or label-free vision-language data and dual objectives that preserve perception while transferring reasoning behavior.
Reconstruct the model update from the scaled subspaces and add it back to the base model.

paras: The paper changes the granularity of model merging. Instead of one merge weight per layer or one direct addition of a whole reasoning update, it learns a separate merge scale for each decomposed subspace inside the update.
object.object: the internal directions transferred during model merging

hidden.name: which update subspaces help reasoning without hurting vision
paras: The hidden quantity is the usefulness of each subspace in the reasoning task vector. Some subspaces may carry the patterns that support multi-step reasoning. Others may encode shifts that interfere with image grounding or linguistic alignment. The merge procedure does not know that decomposition in advance.

FRISM estimates it by learning coefficients on top of the decomposed update while monitoring vision-language behavior. If increasing one subspace improves reasoning while preserving perception, that coefficient can grow because the training objective rewards that tradeoff. If another subspace degrades image understanding, its coefficient should stay small even if it came from the reasoning model.

heat.caption: The target is not the largest subspace by size alone, but the subspace whose effect improves reasoning while keeping visual behavior intact.

reads.html: The model is trying to discover which parts of the reasoning update are worth importing and which parts should be held back because they would blur or distort the original visual skills.
FRISM learns subspace-level merge coefficients over an SVD decomposition of the reasoning task vector so transfer can be selective rather than layer-global.

mechanism.h2: Why subspace-level merging can preserve vision
paras: A whole-layer merge is blunt because it assumes a layer acts as one indivisible unit. In practice, the model update inside a layer spans several directions. Singular value decomposition helps separate those directions into ranked components, which makes selective control possible. The ranking is useful because large components often carry dominant structure, but FRISM does not assume that every large component is safe. It learns the scale of each component from downstream behavior.

The self-distillation step matters because the merged model needs a teacher signal without requiring new labeled reasoning data. On common vision-language data, the system can preserve desirable outputs from the base model while also pulling in reasoning behavior from the reasoning model. The dual objective is important because pure reasoning transfer would ignore perception, while pure perception preservation would block most transfer.

This design can improve the reasoning-perception tradeoff because the merge becomes targeted. Instead of importing every change made by the reasoning model, FRISM imports the parts that appear compatible with the visual tasks and suppresses the rest. That reduces the chance that improved chain-of-thought ability comes from overwriting the image-grounded computations the base model already learned.

stages.s: Base vision-language model and reasoning-adapted model
Decompose the update into ordered subspaces
Learn subspace-specific merge coefficients with dual objectives
Merged model whose reasoning improves while visual grounding stays intact because harmful subspaces were held back

math.words: The reasoning update is decomposed into subspace components, and each component receives its own learned scale before the components are summed back into the merged model.
math.equation: Delta_theta = sum_k alpha_k * subspace_k ; theta_merged = theta_base + Delta_theta
symbols: the k-th subspace component from the decomposed reasoning task vector
the learned merge scale for that subspace

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Suppose a reasoning update is decomposed into three subspaces.
Subspace 1 improves multi-step answer selection and gets scale 0.9.
Subspace 2 slightly harms object grounding and gets scale 0.2.
Subspace 3 has mixed effects and gets scale 0.5.
The final merge imports most of subspace 1, a small share of subspace 2, and a moderate share of subspace 3.
That reconstructed update differs from a layer-level merge because the harmful portion is not forced in at full strength.

math.note: The decomposition is a tool for controllable transfer: it turns one coarse update into several parts that can be rewarded or restrained separately.

charts.title: Coarse layer-level merge
charts.note: A coarse merge can import reasoning gains, but it often damages visual ability because every direction in the layer-level update is transferred together.

charts.title: FRISM subspace-level merge
charts.note: Selective subspace scaling improves the tradeoff because the merge can retain reasoning-helpful directions while damping perception-harming ones. The values are illustrative summaries of the reported trend.

items.b: Useful and harmful effects may share a subspace.
items.html: SVD does not guarantee a perfect separation of reasoning and perception, so one component can still mix both effects because the decomposition is mathematical rather than task-aware.

items.b: Self-distillation can preserve the wrong behavior.
items.html: If the teacher behavior on vision-language data is itself biased or weak on certain visual tasks, preservation pressure may lock in those weaknesses because the merge is trained to imitate them.

items.b: Subspace scales may overfit the merge dataset.
items.html: If coefficient learning sees only a narrow data pattern, the selected tradeoff can look good in that slice while transferring poorly to unseen reasoning or perception tasks.
The method is strongest when the merge data covers both visual grounding and reasoning behavior well enough that the coefficient learner can distinguish helpful transfer from harmful drift.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Take a small vision-language model and a version of the same model adapted for harder reasoning tasks. Compute the task vector between them, then compare a coarse layer-level merge with a subspace-level merge that learns separate coefficients after an SVD step. Evaluate on both visual grounding tasks and reasoning tasks.

Plot the learned coefficients and show examples where the coarse merge changes a visually grounded answer while the subspace merge keeps it. The demo should prove that fine-grained control over transferred directions changes the reasoning-perception tradeoff in a measurable way.
demo.closing: The demo must show that the gain comes from selective transfer of internal directions, not merely from adding more reasoning weight changes everywhere.
